# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book is written for medical students who have just spent weeks learning how human cells work:
membranes, organelles, the electron transport chain, the path from DNA to protein. A microbe faces
many of the problems a human cell faces: it needs a boundary, a source of energy and a way to copy
itself. Its solutions differ from those of human cells, and drugs and the immune system act on those
differences.

Microbiology is often taught as a long sequence of organisms, each with its own list of facts. The
2026 revision of the microbiology core knowledge objectives for medical schools recommends moving away
from that approach [@bauler2026objectives]. Instead, we ask the same six questions of every kind of
microbe, starting with what it is built from and ending with what it has that human cells lack (see
[*The microbial world*](chapters/foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-questions)). Bacteria,
viruses, fungi and parasites answer them differently, and those answers explain how each group causes
disease and how it is detected and controlled.

## Contents and scope

The book is divided by kind of microbe, after a shared foundation:

::: {.concept-tree}
[Parts of the book]{.tree-title}

- [Foundations](chapters/foundations/index.qmd): ideas shared by every kind of microbe (scale,
  hosts, transmission, detection and control)
- [The bacterial world](chapters/bacteria/index.qmd): how bacteria work, then the bacterial groups
- [The viral world](chapters/viruses/index.qmd): how viruses work, then the viral groups
- [The fungal world](chapters/fungi/index.qmd): fungal principles and groups
- [The parasitic world](chapters/parasites/index.qmd): life cycles, protozoa and helminths
- [Across the worlds](chapters/across/comparing-worlds.qmd): the six questions compared
:::

Each world opens with chapters on how that kind of microbe works and then takes its groups in turn,
asking the six questions of each.

Where each infection occurs in the body, how it is diagnosed and how it is treated are left out,
because those topics come later in the organ-system blocks, and pharmacology will teach the drugs.
The aim here is a framework that makes those later facts easier to place. A named organism appears as
an example of a trait, and organisms usually appear in contrasting pairs, because students who compare
two cases side by side apply the principle to new cases more often than students who study each case
alone [@alfieri2013contrasting].

Each technical term is defined where it first appears in a chapter, and all of them are collected in
the [glossary](glossary.qmd).

## How to use the interactive parts

| Activity | What to do |
|---|---|
| Predict, then reveal | Commit to a prediction before the answer appears. Guess even when unsure: a wrong prediction followed by feedback still helps learning |
| Contrast pairs | Find the one feature that separates two similar organisms, then sort descriptions between them |
| Check your understanding | Answer a short quiz at the end of each chapter. Most questions ask why something happens |
| Flashcards | Review the chapter's ideas over the following weeks; the deck spaces each card further apart as it is answered correctly |
| Practise | Work through a short branching case using the chapter's ideas |

Answers are saved only in the reader's own browser. Nothing is sent anywhere, and there is no login.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Draft
This is a pilot. The foundation chapters are complete. In the bacterial world, the chapters on
structure, genetics and detection, *A map of the bacteria* and *Gram-positive cocci* are written in
full; the other chapters show their planned content. All content is awaiting review by
teaching staff, and notes for teaching staff are in the appendix.
:::
